result:
I now have the full path traced. Here's the whole life of an overdue-issue alert.

## What starts the check

`src/instrumentation.ts` runs once per server process boot and calls `registerEventHandlers()` (wiring every event-bus subscriber, including the notification fan-out) and `startScheduler()` from `src/server/jobs/scheduler.ts`. That scheduler sets a `setInterval` (`TICK_INTERVAL_MS = 60_000`, unref'd) that calls `tick(now)` every minute.

`tick()` walks `CADENCE_MINUTES`, and for `"overdue-issues"` the cadence is 60 minutes. `isDue()` compares `now` against the `lastRunAt` map entry for that job kind; once an hour has elapsed it calls `enqueue()` (`src/server/jobs/queue.ts`) with a job id derived from the current minute bucket (so a re-entrant tick can't double-enqueue), then immediately calls `drain()`, which dispatches the queued job through `runHandler()`'s switch statement to `runOverdueIssueJob` in `src/server/jobs/overdue-issue-job.ts`.

There's a second, independent entry point: `src/app/api/cron/overdue/route.ts` is a `POST` handler (secured by `assertCronSecret`) meant to be hit by an external cron trigger (e.g. a platform cron), which calls `runOverdueIssueJob(new Date())` directly, bypassing the queue entirely. Both paths converge on the same job function.

## Narrowing the set of issues that count

`runOverdueIssueJob` first checks `shouldFilterArchived(LIVE_ONLY)` from `src/lib/soft-delete.ts` as a sanity guard — if archive-scoping is misconfigured it logs a warning and skips the whole sweep rather than risk announcing archived issues. It then pulls org ids in batches of 50 via `usageRepo.listOrgIdsForRollup`, and for each org calls `issueRepo.listOverdueIssues(orgId, stamp)` (`src/server/repositories/issue-repository.ts:507`). That query is where the real narrowing happens: it filters to the org, excludes archived issues (`livePredicate`), requires a non-null `dueAt` that is `lt(now)`, and restricts `status` to the still-open set (`backlog`, `todo`, `in_progress`, `in_review`) — so `done`/`cancelled` issues, even if their due date passed, never come back.

## What the job does and doesn't own

For each returned issue, the job does an in-process dedupe against a module-level `Set<string>` called `reported` (comment: "Issues already announced this process's lifetime") — if the issue id is already in that set, it's skipped. Otherwise it calls `emit("issue.overdue", {...})` on the typed event bus (`src/lib/event-bus.ts`) with the org, issue, project, due date and assignee, then adds the issue id to `reported`. The job's docstring is explicit about scope: "The job owns no notification logic: it announces the fact, and whoever cares... reacts on the bus." It only tracks processed/failed counts (`JobResult`) and logs a failure per issue if `emit` throws — it does not know or care who gets told or how.

## What stops repeat announcements

Two layers of dedupe exist. The first is the `reported` Set in `overdue-issue-job.ts` — since the issue's status/dueAt don't change just because it's overdue, every subsequent hourly sweep would otherwise re-find and re-announce the same issue; the Set makes each issue eligible for exactly one `emit` per process lifetime (there's a `resetOverdueTracking()` export used only by tests to clear it between scenarios). The second, downstream layer is standard "unread" semantics: once `notify()` (see below) writes a notification row, that row stays unread until the recipient reads it or a digest run marks it read — nothing re-inserts a new row for the same overdue issue, so there's no duplicate notification to begin with. Together this is why the alert fires once, not every tick.

## From event to one specific person's chosen channels

`src/server/services/notification-service.ts` calls `registerFanOut()` at module load (imported transitively via `event-registry.ts`'s `import "./notification-service"`), which subscribes to `"issue.overdue"`. The handler guards `if (payload.assigneeId === null) return` — an unassigned overdue issue announces nothing to anyone — then calls `notify(orgId, "issue_overdue", [payload.assigneeId], {...})` with exactly the one assignee as recipient.

`notify()` is where "the channels they chose" comes in: for that recipient it calls `preferenceRepo.getPreference(orgId, recipientId, "issue_overdue")` (`notification-preference-repository.ts`), then `resolveChannels(preference, flags)`. If the user has no explicit preference row, it falls back to `DEFAULT_CHANNELS = ["in_app", "email"]`; otherwise it builds the channel list from `preference.inApp` and `preference.email` (with `email` further gated by `!preference.digestOnly || isEnabled("digest_email", flags)`). If the resolved channel list is empty (everything muted), that recipient is skipped — no row is written at all. Otherwise `notificationRepo.insertNotifications` writes one row (`src/server/db/schema/notifications.ts`) carrying the recipient id, kind, title/body/href, and the serialized `channels` array.

From there, delivery is channel-specific: the `in_app` channel is satisfied just by that row existing — `notification-bell.tsx` and `notification-list.tsx` read it back via `countUnread`/`listNotifications`. The `email` channel isn't sent immediately in this codebase; it's only realized later for users who opted into `digestOnly` (`listDigestSubscribers` in the preference repo), via the separate hourly `runDigestEmailJob` (`src/server/jobs/digest-email-job.ts`), which calls `buildDigest`/`renderDigest` (`digest-service.ts`) and `sendEmail` — and marks the underlying notifications read so the digest, too, never repeats itself.
